PD2-P4-4.note: Mentzel's crowing-bookworm description is strange, so 'curious' modifies the characterization as peculiar.

exclusions.A: When one reads that he heard the bookworm crow like a cock, and said, "I knew not whether some local fowl was clamoring or whether there was but a beating in my ears," one can not help wondering if there was not something defective in his ear drums; but further on he says, "I perceived, in the paper whereon I was writing, a little insect that ceased not to carol like very chanticleer, until taking a magnifying glass I assiduously observed him."
exclusions.B: From this one concludes that if the fault were not with his hearing, by which some well-known sounds made by book insects seemed to him like the crowing of a cock, an altogether different cock from the kind we know must have lived in his day.
exclusions.C: A curious and interesting characterization of some species of book insects has come to us in the writings of Christian Mentzel, the German naturalist and philologist, who lived in the seventeenth century.
exclusions.D: Reaction against these weird and fantastical accounts is indicated by the question, not infrequently asked, "Are there such things as bookworms?"

PD2-P4-5.note: The author treats Mentzel's crowing-cock comparison with wry humor (his ear drums, or a different kind of cock in his day), not respect, suspicion of fabrication, indignation or real worry. A (respect for his care) is the strongest distractor but is undercut by the joking tone.
